description: Space is what brought us together! We love digging into research, learning new things, and turning big ideas into creative stories. This time, we’re exploring the gear NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars, the footprints of humanity beyond Earth. Our dream is to earn a certificate from NASA, and of course, a win would be the cherry on top!
summary:
Discovery Atlas: Meet the Machines We Left Behind

Discovery Atlas is a mobile app that lets kids aged 6–12 discover NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. Players create their own astronaut, choose a robot guide, and travel a solar-system map. Each lost machine appears as a character pinned on its planet. Our first story is Spirit and Opportunity, the Mars rovers built for a three-month mission that kept working for years. It is told as a comic, or as an animated video, in the voice of a storyteller.

After each story, kids play four challenge levels tied to what they just read. A green progress bar fills as they answer, and they earn a badge for completing the story. Every fact comes from NASA mission pages, and our invented dialogue is clearly separate from the verified facts.

The app turns forgotten hardware into characters children care about. It explains how the rovers worked: solar power, cameras, rock-grinding tools, and the search for ancient water. It also shows why every machine we leave behind still teaches us something. We are also planning a facts mode for older readers and parents.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Discovery Atlas is a mobile-first app for kids aged 6–12 that tells the stories of NASA machines left behind on the Moon and Mars. A child creates an astronaut (five suits and a name), picks a robot guide, and explores a solar-system map where Mars and the Moon are open. Each planet has pins, and each pin is a lost machine, such as Sojourner, Ingenuity, Apollo hardware and Surveyor. Our first complete story is Spirit & Opportunity, told as a vertical comic. After reading, the child plays four challenges tied to the story: ordering the rover’s parts, matching discoveries to rovers, driving a rover through a crater, and clearing a dust storm off its solar panels. Stars are earned per level, finishing all four marks the machine as found and its pin turns green, and a certificate unlocks. Progress is saved on the device.

What benefits does it have?
Children learn how real missions worked (solar power, cameras, rock-grinding tools, the search for ancient water) by reading and playing. The app is fully bilingual (English and Arabic with right-to-left layout), has large touch targets and nothing frightening.

What is the intended impact?
We want kids to see forgotten hardware as characters with stories, so they remember why we explore. The app is built to grow: 15 more machines are already placed on the maps and waiting for their stories.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?
Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/Radix UI, Framer Motion, Zustand, Cairo and Baloo Bhaijaan 2 fonts, and Playwright for automated testing. We used Claude Code Pro, Manus, ChatGPT and v0.dev to build and iterate. We used Gemini to generate comic backgrounds, and Figma for design.

How is it creative?
The lost machines are the characters, and the child is the astronaut with their own robot guide. A glowing “signal line” runs through the comic story. The challenges are rebuilt from the story, so every game teaches one real mission fact.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Age-appropriate language and short, forgiving levels for 6–12.
  • Accuracy: facts come from NASA mission pages, and invented dialogue is kept separate from verified facts.
  • Accessibility: two languages, big buttons, and difficulty softened after testing.
  • Scope: one complete story with a structure ready for more.
  • Team: five members, covering backend, graphic design, content creation, Flutter development, video editing, and project and business management.
